1:
The houses come first, and nobody reads them quite alike. Ellicott makes it a palace, the plural being intensive, and thinks the alternative less likely, that fresh quarters were needed for additional wives; David had Egyptian and Babylonian precedent for palace-building. Wesley takes the opposite view, a palace of many apartments for his several wives and children, and explains the new tent by David's intention to build the temple forthwith rather than fetch the old tabernacle from Gibeon. Gill keeps to the fabric, a royal palace with its apartments and the outhouses its officers needed, raised with the masons and carpenters Hiram had sent. Ellicott places that tent within the palace precincts and notes the old tabernacle remained at Gibeon under Zadok, so Abiathar probably ministered before the ark in the new one. Henry takes the juxtaposition for a lesson: wherever we build for ourselves we must make room for the ark, for a church in the house.

Why the Levites and no one else is the chapter's real subject. Henry hears the admission of the previous failure, a good work undertaken but God not sought after the due order; it is not enough to do what is good, he says, we must do it well, and when we have suffered for our irregularities we must learn to be more regular. He recalls that the Kohathites bore it on their shoulders in ordinary marches and were allotted no wagons, while on extraordinary occasions the priests carried it; the rule was express, yet David forgot it and set the ark on a cart, so that even those very knowing in the word of God have it not always so ready as were to be wished. Ellicott cites the appointments in Numbers and the plainer words of Deuteronomy and calls this enunciation of the law a tacit acknowledgment that it had not been observed before, adding that the older account has the ark carried by bearers without noticing they were Levites. Delitzsch agrees and quotes Bertheau, that the new arrangement expressly admits a cart to have been contrary to the law. Clarke is blunter: David should have thought of this sooner, and the breach upon Uzza would have been prevented.

The gathering is read as representative rather than literal. Ellicott notes that the parallel does not name Jerusalem as the meeting-place and that only a full representation of the people can be meant; he also marks then as a genuine note of time, the end of the three months the ark had stood elsewhere. Gill says the chief and heads of the people, and observes that from here the chapter is an account of the Levites employed. Both Ellicott and Delitzsch read the second assembly as a separate conference with the priestly order about its own part, and both identify the sons of Aaron as the two high priests then in office, Zadok of the line of Eleazar and Abiathar of Ithamar.

Then the chiefs are counted out. Ellicott explains the proportions: Kohath stands first as the senior clan, to which Aaron's own house belonged, and there are four Kohathite houses to one each of Merari and Gershom because Kohath was the elder line with special charge of the ark. Delitzsch sets the three principal heads against the three sons of Levi, Uriel over the Kohathites, Asaiah over the Merarites and Joel over the Gershonites, each with his brethren. Wesley alone takes the sons of the fifth verse for those of Amram or Izhar, since Kohath's other children are named separately below.
7: The three remaining Kohathite houses are named, and Ellicott alone comments on them. Elzaphan he identifies as a son of Uzziel, who was Kohath's fourth son, so that Shemaiah stood at the head of that family in David's time; Hebron he makes Kohath's third son. The sons of Uzziel then set him a small problem, since Exodus names three of them, Mishael, Elzaphan and Zithri, and the family of Elzaphan has already been represented two verses earlier. He concludes that the phrase here must stand for the two remaining Uzzielite houses, which may have amalgamated into one, and that since Elzaphan is mentioned first the elder line of Mishael may have become extinct. Later lists in the same book, he adds, imply the existence of only two Uzzielite stocks.
11:
The eight chiefs are summoned, and Ellicott makes their names the point. Zadok and Abiathar were of coordinate rank as representing the two priestly lines, though Wesley ranks them as high priest and second priest. Ellicott then reads the whole list etymologically: Zadok imports just, Abiathar that the Father excels, Shemaiah that Jah heareth, Eliel that God and none else is God, Amminadab that the Clansman is bounteous. So the names of the men who conducted this religious event expressed, to themselves and others, that the Lord is righteous and the bestower of all excellence, that he alone is God, and that he hears prayer as a gracious Father.

Then they are told to sanctify themselves, being heads of their fathers' houses. Ellicott observes that special purifications appear to have been prescribed for all sacrifice and worship, the requisites being to bathe, to wash or change the garments, and to keep aloof from whatever was reckoned defiling; all of it needful, he says, to teach Israel that the All-pure requires purity in his worshippers. He also marks the title given the ark here, a solemn one used by way of warning where the earlier chapters had the simpler ark of God, and takes God of Israel to signal that the undertaking is national and the nation's welfare hangs on its due performance, Israel's vocation being a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, as the chronicler has well understood. Gill adds only that they sanctified themselves as ordered and in the manner they should.

On why the breach came, three witnesses abandon the English together: the Authorised Version supplies a verb, that they had not done it at the first, and none of the three who examine the clause accepts it. Ellicott reads the Hebrew to mean that on the first occasion it was not they, the heads of the Levitical houses, who carried up the ark, but Uzza and Ahio, and notes that the phrase so rendered occurs here only. Delitzsch gives the same sense, remarking that the predicate is wanting but easily supplied from the context, and that the contracted form of the opening words is unique. Gill rejects the supplement his own version directs and reads rather that they were not there at the first, when the ark came as far as the house of Obed-edom, and were not employed as was their business. Ellicott adds what the irregularity was, a cart instead of the shoulders and staves, and that even the Kohathites were forbidden to touch any holy thing, as Uzza had ventured to do.

The due order then draws from Ellicott an argument with nothing to do with grammar. It has been said, he reports, that the sanctity of institutions, as opposed to the sanctity of a people under a righteous God, is the leading idea of these books; he answers that it would be hard to show how the sanctity of a people is secured, or the government of a righteous God realised, except in and through divine institutions. As there is a due order by which God rules the physical world, so there is a corresponding order in the spiritual; there are positive institutions in Christianity as well as in Mosaism, and if the divine authority of the one is abolished, why not the other? The bearing itself the rest explain mechanically. Clarke has the staves pass through the rings and rest on the shoulders, the ark resting on them as a sedan rests on its poles; Delitzsch names the flexible pole used for carrying burdens and distinguishes it from the Pentateuch's own term; Gill supplies the reason from Maimonides, that shoulders were required rather than a carriage both for the honour of the ark and lest its structure be damaged. Ellicott closes by noting that the statement anticipates the procession described later, such brief summaries being very common in Hebrew narrative.
16:
The singers are stationed, and the three precentors named. Ellicott reads the order as a command to the chiefs to assign places to their clansmen, and works the last clause hard: grammar would let the participle sounding refer to the musicians, to all the instruments, or to the cymbals alone, and he prefers the cymbals for the special sense of the verb, translating harps and lutes and clashing cymbals, to swell the sound for gladness. Heman, Asaph and Ethan he makes precentors of three Levitical choirs, one from each division of the tribe; Clarke calls them the three chief musicians of David's time,, and Gill adds that Heman was Samuel's grandson and that Ben drops from the list, Azaziah seeming to stand in his room. Delitzsch sorts the three choirs by instrument instead, the first three on brazen cymbals, Benaiah with seven more on psalteries, and the last six on lutes.

Two musical terms then defeat most of them. Ellicott is confident: harps after the mode of maidens, probably soprano compass, and lutes after the mode of the eighth, an octave below the tenor. Clarke canvasses instead of deciding, allowing that the first may mean virgins or women singers whom these men accompanied, while the Vulgate has them singing secret things or mysteries, probably prophetic hymns; for the second he lists an instrument sounding an octave or strung with eight strings, an octave for a song of victory, and the eighth band of musicians, those with the strongest voices. Wesley declines the question, calling these perhaps names of instruments or of tunes whose certain signification is not now known. Delitzsch concurs: the words plainly denote different keys in singing but are obscure, our acquaintance with Hebrew music being too small to interpret them.

Chenaniah divides them two against two. Clarke makes him the master singer who gave the key and the time, skilful in music and powerful in voice, perhaps the precentor; Wesley makes him moderator of the music, instructing the singers when and how to lift up their voices, change their notes or make their stops. Ellicott denies it on three grounds: the context, since Heman, Asaph and Ethan were already the conductors of singing; that Chenaniah is nowhere else associated with music; and that the word, used of Levites, means bearing. He makes him captain of the Levites in the carriage of the ark, conducting the bearing because skilled in the regulations for it,. Delitzsch takes the same side, rendering it prince of the Levites for the bearing and teacher in bearing, pointing to the title given the man later, and allowing that the word is very variously interpreted.

The warders and trumpeters close the muster, and Ellicott reconstructs the file from them: the three master-singers with two bands of seven, the marshal of the bearers, two warders, and seven priests with trumpets. Wesley explains what the warders were for, to keep the door of the tent so no unallowed person should press in and touch the ark, and to attend it on the road and guard it from the touch of profane hands, two walking before and two behind. Ellicott argues that these two are probably not the minstrels of the same names, since the procession puts the minstrels two places ahead of them, since one name differs in form and meaning from the other, and since a second Obed-edom need not surprise in books where names recur so often. On the trumpets he notes that silver clarions were blown by priests for calling the assembly and the journeying of the camps, and guesses the seven walked immediately before the ark as at Jericho. Wesley ends on the novelty of the whole thing: praising God by musical instruments had not hitherto been in use, but David instituted it by divine direction and added it to the other ordinances of that dispensation.
25:
That God helped the Levites is where the comment gathers. Henry makes four things of it: that it is good to notice providence even in what falls within our natural powers, since without help we could not stir a step; that the bearers, remembering the breach upon Uzza, were ready to tremble as they took up the ark, so that helping them meant silencing their fears; and that God's ministers who bear the vessels of the Lord have special need of such help, which Wesley repeats almost word for word. Gill says the same from the other side: not bodily strength, which the burden hardly required, but help to carry it cheerfully and without error. Ellicott puts it as an inference the bearers drew: God had been adverse to those who conducted the ark before, and six paces borne now without a sign of wrath called forth the offerings of hearts relieved from a dread which only ceased to haunt them when the event proved it groundless.

The sacrifice sets a problem Ellicott works at length. Samuel has oxen and fatlings offered when the bearers had gone six paces; this text has seven bullocks and seven rams. He reports a proposal that the two accounts describe different offerings, Samuel meaning that a beast was killed at every six paces by priests stationed along the course while this text gives a final sacrifice at the end, and calls it incredible, not least for supposing priests the narrative never mentions. His conclusion is that the offerings are probably not different at all, the narrative being generally parallel and the chronicler having perhaps paraphrased the older text to explain it. Clarke keeps to the motive: seeing no breach made among them as in Uzza's case, they sacrificed in gratitude for their preservation and the acceptance of their labour.

Whether David was clothed or dancing is a textual question two witnesses answer alike. Ellicott notes that Samuel has David dancing before Jehovah with all his might, and thinks the Hebrew here a corruption or intentional alteration, the word for clothed being an Aramaic one that could easily displace the rare word for dancing. Delitzsch sees the same, the two differing only in their last two letters, and reports a conjecture that a copyist who remembered David's clothing wrote one for the other while the words now read as a robe of byssus were guessed at because illegible; but he will not accept it while other discrepancies stand unexplained. Clarke takes the linen at face value and identifies the stuff as byssus, probably the beard of a species of muscle found along the Mediterranean; he had seen gloves made of it, a deep dark yellow inclining to lilac, and observes the material is not heard of in Israel before David. Ellicott adds that the garment was one worn by persons of rank, and corrects the master of the song to the chief of the bearing. Wesley thinks the ephod repeated because it was unusual for one who was no Levite to wear a Levitical garment; Gill says the king, being among the singers, was dressed as they were.

The procession and its sour note close the chapter. Ellicott tidies the instruments, reading trumpet for cornet and clarions for the straight trumpets, and noting the rest of the verse is wanting in Samuel though every instrument it adds is already named. On the final verse he finds a modernised form of the older text, two common words put for two obsolete ones, the word for playing denoting dancing combined with singing; Michal despised the king, he says, because he seemed to have forgotten what his rank required. Clarke refuses the question here and sends the reader to his note on the parallel, where David's conduct is vindicated and the nature of Michal's disgrace is hinted at but left, he says, to the reader's own determination.
